CM-11 (User-installed Software) directly establishes policies governing installation of software by users and enforces those policies, fully preventing the installation and execution of unauthorized software.

CM-7 (Least Functionality) prohibits or restricts specific software, ports, protocols, and services, helping to prevent unauthorized software but not directly addressing user installation or runtime execution enforcement.
SI-16 (Memory Protection) implements controls to protect system memory from unauthorized code execution, addressing part of the framework item but not installation prevention.
SI-3 (Malicious Code Protection) detects and eradicates malicious code at entry and exit points, supporting prevention of unauthorized software execution.
SI-7 (Software, Firmware, and Information Integrity) employs integrity verification tools to detect unauthorized changes to software, supporting prevention of unauthorized installations.

PM-6 (Measures of Performance) develops, monitors, and reports on information security and privacy measures of performance, partially addressing performance monitoring of secure development practices.
CP-2 (Contingency Plan) addresses contingency roles and responsibilities, supporting coordination and stakeholder communication during recovery activities.
IR-8 (Incident Response Plan) describes the structure and organization of the incident response capability and a high-level approach that can encompass stakeholder communication during recovery.
IR-1 (Policy and Procedures) establishes the incident response policy framework that can define approved methods and messaging for public communications during recovery.
IR-8 (Incident Response Plan) provides the structure and organization of the incident response capability, which can include approved communication methods and messaging for public updates.
IR-1 establishes the overarching incident response policy and procedures that authorise and govern the plan execution but does not contain operational recovery content.

CP-2 requires the contingency plan to identify essential mission functions, provide recovery objectives, restoration priorities, and metrics—directly supporting selection, scoping, and prioritisation of recovery actions.
CP-4 tests the contingency plan using defined tests and initiates corrective actions—validating that selected/scoped/prioritised recovery actions actually work when performed.
SC-28 protects the integrity of information at rest, providing a baseline protective measure for backup assets that supports later integrity verification prior to use in restoration.
SI-2 requires testing of software and firmware updates for effectiveness and potential side effects before installation, contributing to integrity assurance practices applied to restoration assets.

SI-7 employs integrity verification tools to detect unauthorized changes to software, firmware, and information—directly supporting the verification of integrity for backups (information) before restoration.
CP-2 requires identification of essential mission and business functions and associated contingency requirements, providing the foundation for considering critical mission functions post-incident.
PM-28 documents assumptions, constraints, priorities, and trade-offs for risk assessments/responses/monitoring, supporting consistent risk framing when establishing post-incident operational norms.

RA-9 performs criticality analysis to identify critical system components and functions at decision points in the SDLC, directly supporting identification of critical mission functions for post-incident norms.
CP-2 (Contingency Plan) requires a plan identifying recovery objectives, restoration priorities and metrics, supporting the restoration of systems and services.
CP-4 (Contingency Plan Testing) tests the effectiveness and readiness of the contingency plan, helping confirm that normal operating status has been achieved.
CP-6 (Alternate Storage Site) establishes agreements and equivalent controls at an alternate storage site, enabling retrieval of backup information needed for restoration.
CP-7 (Alternate Processing Site) provides alternate processing capabilities that enable the transfer and resumption of system operations for essential functions during recovery.
CP-9 (System Backup) requires backups of user-level, system-level information and documentation, which is foundational to enabling the restoration of systems and services.

IR-4 (Incident Handling) explicitly includes recovery as part of the incident lifecycle (preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, and recovery), supporting the restoration aspect.
SI-7 (Software, Firmware, and Information Integrity) requires employing integrity verification tools to detect unauthorized changes, directly supporting verification of integrity for restored assets.
SR-10 (Inspection of Systems or Components) requires inspecting systems/components to detect tampering, supporting verification of integrity for restored assets.
AU-11 (Audit Record Retention) retains audit records to support after-the-fact investigations, enabling the availability of incident-related documentation.
IR-5 (Incident Monitoring) requires tracking and documenting incidents across the incident lifecycle, directly supporting the completion of incident-related documentation.
IR-6 (Incident Reporting) requires personnel to report suspected incidents and to report incident information to authorities, contributing to completeness of incident-related documentation.

AU-6 (Audit Record Review, Analysis, and Reporting) requires review and analysis of system audit records 'for indications of inappropriate or unusual activity,' which is foundational to incident and root cause analysis. However, it focuses on audit records rather than the full scope of incident analysis.
IR-5 (Incident Monitoring) tracks and documents incidents, providing the data inputs that enable root cause analysis. It supports but does not itself perform root cause analysis.

AU-12 (Audit Record Generation) provides audit record generation capability for defined event types, supporting the recording of actions performed. It enables recording but does not itself preserve integrity and provenance.

AU-2 (Event Logging) identifies the types of events that the system is capable of logging, providing the foundation for what gets recorded during an investigation. It supports the recording component but is not itself the recording mechanism.

AU-3 (Content of Audit Records) ensures audit records contain information about 'What type of event occurred,' 'When,' 'Where,' 'Source,' 'Outcome,' and 'Identity'—recording actions performed during investigative activities. It supports recording but is scoped to system audit events rather than all investigation actions.

AU-9 (Protection of Audit Information) protects audit information and audit logging tools from 'unauthorized access, modification, and deletion' and alerts on detection, directly addressing integrity preservation of records. It supports provenance preservation but is focused on audit information specifically.

SI-7 (Software, Firmware, and Information Integrity) employs integrity verification tools to detect unauthorized changes, supporting the integrity preservation aspect of investigation records. It is an enabling control for integrity but does not directly address investigation record provenance.

AC-16 (Security and Privacy Attributes) provides the means to associate types of security and privacy attributes with attribute values for information, supporting provenance tracking and integrity of data through attribute association.
AU-12 (Audit Record Generation) provides the generation capability for event types, which is the mechanism by which incident data and metadata are collected. It enables collection of the data.

AU-2 (Event Logging) identifies and coordinates the types of events the system logs, defining what data and metadata are collected. It supports the collection requirement but is scoped to audit event types.

AU-3 (Content of Audit Records) ensures audit records include the data and metadata fields needed (what, when, where, source, outcome, identity), directly addressing collection of incident data and metadata content.

AU-9 (Protection of Audit Information) protects audit information from unauthorized access, modification, and deletion, preserving the integrity of collected incident data and metadata. It supports provenance preservation as well through these protections.

IR-5 (Incident Monitoring) explicitly tracks and documents incidents, directly collecting incident data and metadata across the incident lifecycle. It contributes to collection but does not address integrity and provenance preservation.
AU-6 review and analysis of audit records for 'potential impact' supplies evidence used to estimate magnitude, but is general audit review rather than dedicated incident magnitude validation.
IR-5 'Track and document incidents' provides the ongoing record-keeping that enables analysts to revisit and validate an incident's magnitude, but does not itself perform the estimation.
SI-4 detects 'attacks and indicators of potential attacks,' providing the raw detection data needed to scope an incident, but does not itself estimate or validate magnitude.
IR-8 Incident Response Plan establishes the structure and approach for incident response, which would include notification procedures; enabling but not performing notification itself.

AU-16 'coordinate audit information among external organizations' is focused on audit-related information across boundaries, supporting broader cross-stakeholder information sharing but for audit context specifically.

PM-16 establishes 'a cross-organization information-sharing capability for threat intelligence,' directly supporting sharing of security information with designated stakeholders, but scoped to threat intelligence.

AU-16 employs methods for coordinating audit information among external organizations when audit information crosses organizational boundaries, enabling joint incident analysis with relevant third parties.

CA-3 approves and manages the exchange of information between the system and other systems using interconnection security agreements, MOUs, SLAs, etc., establishing the governance basis for third-party coordination during incidents.

IR-4 implements the incident handling capability and explicitly coordinates incident handling activities with contingency planning and other organizational activities, directly supporting the coordination requirement.
AU-11 retains audit records to provide support for after-the-fact investigations of incidents, preserving evidence used in triage and validation activities.
AU-3 ensures audit records contain event type, time, location, source, outcome, and identity information, supplying the structured data needed to triage and validate incidents.
AU-6 review and analysis of audit records for indications of inappropriate or unusual activity provides supporting evidence used to triage and validate incident reports.
RA-2 security categorization of the system and the information it processes establishes baseline impact levels that inform incident categorization decisions.
IR-8 develops the incident response plan that describes the structure and organization of the IR capability, including escalation roles and thresholds.

CP-10 (System Recovery and Reconstitution) provides for recovery and reconstitution 'to a known state within organization-defined time period consistent with recovery time and recovery point objectives,' enabling recovery operations. It supports but is not specifically about initiating incident recovery criteria.

CP-2 (Contingency Plan) identifies essential mission and business functions and provides recovery objectives, restoration priorities, and metrics. It supports the broader recovery framework but is focused on continuity rather than incident-driven recovery criteria.
IR-3 tests the effectiveness of the incident response capability, validating that containment procedures work as designed, but does not directly contain incidents.
IR-8 Incident Response Plan provides the roadmap and structure that defines how containment activities are executed, enabling but not performing containment.
CP-10 provides recovery and reconstitution of the system 'to a known state... after a disruption, compromise, or failure', which typically follows eradication and confirms the system is clean.
RA-10 threat hunting 'Detect[s], track[s], and disrupt[s] threats that evade existing controls', helping ensure persistent threats are identified and removed as part of eradication.
SC-35 uses components that 'proactively seek to identify network-based malicious code or malicious websites', supporting eradication by surfacing malicious artifacts that must be removed.

SI-2 requires the organization to 'Identify, report, and correct system flaws' and install security updates within defined time periods, which is a primary mechanism for eradicating vulnerabilities exploited during incidents.
SI-3 requires malicious code protection mechanisms that 'detect and eradicate malicious code', covering eradication of malicious-code incidents but not all incident types.
SI-4 monitoring detects attacks, indicators of potential attacks, and unauthorized use, providing the visibility needed to know when eradication actions are complete.
SI-7 uses integrity verification tools and prescribes actions when unauthorized changes are detected, which helps remove attacker artifacts and re-establish a clean state during eradication.
